sections.label: SINGA financing of infrastructure costs
sections.summary: Under the SINGA framework, lumpy infrastructure costs above $4 billion can be financed with long-term debt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Under this SINGA framework, lumpy infrastructure costs greater than $4 billion can be financed using long-term debt.

sections.label: Large long-term infrastructure projects
sections.summary: Projects like the Cross Island Line, Jurong Rail Line and Deep Tunnel Sewerage System are big outlays whose construction may exceed a decade with multi-generational benefits.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Projects like the Cross Island Line, Jurong Rail Line as well as the Deep Tunnel Sewerage System are not only super big-ticket outlays, their constructions may stretch more than a decade with benefits accruing across generations.

sections.label: Conditions for borrowing under SINGA
sections.summary: Borrowing for such expenditures is the next best option but with strict conditions, including a 50-year useful life, a $90 billion gross borrowing limit and an annual interest threshold.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Given these considerations and the current budgetary constraints, I would agree that the next best option would be to borrow for such expenditures – but with strict conditions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: I note the list of qualifying criteria to borrow under SINGA such as the minimal useful life of 50 years and that the projects should support national productivity and achieve economic, environmental and social sustainability goals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: The overall gross borrowing limit of $90 billion ensures that the Government will not run into an excessive debt situation and that we will have the ability to service and repay the debt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: It is also important to impose an annual interest threshold to avoid overly onerous financing costs on future generations, although, in my view, the $5 billion threshold in the Bill appears to be on the high side.

sections.label: Pioneer and Merdeka Generation Packages
sections.summary: In 2015 and 2018 the Government set aside $15 billion from accumulated surplus or current reserves for the PGP and MGP healthcare support.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: In 2015 and 2018, to thank our Pioneer and Merdeka Generations for their sacrifices, the Government set aside a total of $15 billion from the accumulated surplus or current reserves to set up the Pioneer Generation Package (PGP) and Merdeka Generation Package (MGP) to provide healthcare support for our seniors.

sections.label: Sharing infrastructure costs across generations
sections.summary: Because the infrastructure benefits multiple generations, sharing costs across generations through a long-term financing structure is more equitable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: As this infrastructure benefits multiple generations, it is more equitable to share the costs across generations by way of a long-term financing structure.

sections.label: Constitutional amendment on NIR use
sections.summary: In 2009 the Constitution was amended to allow 50% of the NIR to fund current annual Budget spending and help balance each year's Budget.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: With regard to NIR, we amended the Constitution in 2009 to allow 50% of the NIR to be used to fund the current annual Budget spending, to help balance each year's Budget.

sections.label: Long-term cross-generation infrastructure projects
sections.summary: The Cross Island Line, Jurong Rail Line and Deep Tunnel Sewerage System are long-term, cross-generation endeavours benefiting many generations onwards.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Projects like the Cross Island Line, Jurong Rail Line as well as the Deep Tunnel Sewerage System are all long-term, cross-generation endeavours which will benefit many generation onwards.

sections.label: Debt limits and borrowing principles
sections.summary: The Bill sets key principles including a $90 billion borrowing limit and a $5 billion annual interest payment threshold.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Of course, we have the duty to ensure that we do not leave a huge debt to our future generations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: This Bill has also set certain key principles that we must abide by, such as the $90 billion borrowing limit and the $5 billion annual interest payment threshold.

sections.label: Deputy Prime Minister on special purpose borrowing
sections.summary: The Deputy Prime Minister said the Government would study one-off, special purpose borrowing to finance economic investments for post-COVID-19 recovery.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: In his round-up speech, the Deputy Prime Minister replied that the Government would study the possibility of a one-off, special purpose borrowing to finance economic investments to help Singapore emerge stronger from COVID-19.

sections.label: Deploying one-off special purpose borrowings
sections.summary: Special purpose borrowings can be deployed if revenues are insufficient, being one-off and linked to post-COVID-19 recovery and investment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: So, if our revenues are insufficient to fund these investments due to the economic situation being subdued, then we can deploy such special purpose borrowings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: And such special purpose borrowings can also be distinguished from the normal borrowing in that it is one-off, it has a clear nexus with strategies for post-COVID-19 recovery and investment and also help us keep our assets invested.

sections.label: AAA rating and SINGA Bill
sections.summary: A Member asked whether Singapore's AAA rating could be affected by the SINGA Bill and how rating agencies and markets responded.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: — our AAA rating by all three major global rating agencies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: I believe we are amongst the remaining nine countries in world left that continue to enjoy this highest rating.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: So, being a AAA-rated sovereign enables us to borrow from the international market at a risk-free rate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: It also has implications on the borrowing cost of Singapore corporates, as bonds issued by corporates/companies are often benchmarked to the Singapore Government yield curve.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: So, can I ask the Deputy Prime Minister if our AAA rating status could be affected with this SINGA Bill and how have the rating agencies and international market responded to this new move?

sections.label: SINGA project eligibility criteria
sections.summary: SINGA projects must be at least $4 billion, government-owned, used for at least 50 years and important to national interests.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: Projects under SINGA need to be at least $4 billion, with the infrastructure available for use for at least 50 years, owned by the Government and important to national interests.

sections.label: Bill borrowing cap safeguards
sections.summary: The Bill includes safeguards capping overall gross borrowing at $90 billion.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: The Bill includes safeguards that cap the overall gross borrowing at $90 billion.

sections.label: SINGA borrowing cap
sections.summary: Borrowings under SINGA are capped at $90 billion, about 20% of GDP.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: Borrowings under SINGA are capped at $90 billion, about 20% of GDP.

sections.label: GST hike versus interest costs
sections.summary: A two percentage point GST hike is expected to raise $3 billion, but GST would have to be raised 3.3% to cover $5 billion interest costs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: To put things into perspective, the impending GST hike of two percentage points is expected to raise $3 billion in revenue, but GST would have to be raised 3.3% to cover interest costs of $5 billion.

sections.label: Overseas borrowing and forex risk
sections.summary: The Government can raise money outside Singapore in non-Singapore-dollar currency, and the passage asks how it intends to manage foreign exchange risk.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: The Government can raise money outside of Singapore and in a currency other than the Singapore dollars.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: How does the Government intend to manage the foreign exchange risk related to this borrowing?

sections.label: Borrowing limits and interest threshold
sections.summary: The passage raises concern about the $90 billion borrowing limits and $5 billion interest threshold in clause 5, asking how these values were arrived at.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: My first concern has to do with both the total borrowing limits of $90 billion, as well as the interest threshold amount of $5 billion stated in clause 5 of the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: I think it is worth asking how these values were arrived at.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: I also wonder why the interest threshold of $5 billion was chosen which would imply an interest rate of 5.6%, as Minister Heng alluded to.

sections.label: Nationally significant infrastructure definition
sections.summary: Clause 11(2) defines nationally significant infrastructure as having a useful life of at least 50 years upon project completion.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Third, clause 11(2) of the Bill defines nationally significant infrastructure to be one that has a useful life of at least 50 years upon completion of the project.

sections.label: Lower useful life threshold
sections.summary: The speaker says a lower useful life threshold of 35 years seems more reasonable.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: A lower useful life threshold of say, 35 years, strikes me as more reasonable.

sections.label: Infrastructure versus schooling returns
sections.summary: Global infrastructure real long-term returns are 2.6%, while an extra year of schooling returns about 10.2%.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: As an asset class, the expected long-term returns from global infrastructure, net of inflation, is only 2.6%.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In contrast, the real returns to an additional year of schooling is often in the order of 10.2%, almost 10 times as large.

sections.label: Infrastructure and education output gains
sections.summary: A 1% infrastructure capital increase may raise output 7% to 10%, while secondary education gains are 10% to 12%.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: While estimates may differ, one recent study suggests that a 1% increase in infrastructure capital can elevate output by 7% to 10%, not a number to be sniffed at.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: But the comparable increase in Secondary education alone could induce gains of 10% to 12%.

sections.label: SINGA for class sizes and insurance
sections.summary: SINGA could fund smaller language and math classes, keep schools open, and seed a redundancy insurance risk pool.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In my earlier speeches, I spoke about how we could finance smaller class sizes, even if on a limited basis, for languages and math, or to provide additional funding for teaching aides.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: This will allow us to avoid closing or merging schools and instead direct SINGA funds towards keeping schools open, albeit with trimmed-down class sizes.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Similarly, we could use SINGA to seed an initial insurance risk pool, so as to enable us to roll out redundancy insurance without delay and without drawing down on our reserves.

sections.label: SINGA for income-contingent scholarships
sections.summary: SINGA could seed a fund for income-contingent scholarships.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: First, we could use SINGA to seed a fund for income-contingent scholarships, as I mentioned earlier.

sections.label: SINGA vouchers for pre-schools and charter schools
sections.summary: SINGA funds could go to parent vouchers for non-KiFAS-eligible pre-schools and charter schools with non-traditional syllabi.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Second, we could direct SINGA funds towards vouchers that would be applied by parents to send their children to both non-KiFAS-eligible pre-schools as well as charter schools, which are schools allowed to develop non-traditional syllabi that de-emphasise academic testing but, nevertheless, set rigorous, assessable markers for inquiry, innovation, imagination and invention.

sections.label: Act purpose for borrowing
sections.summary: The Act lets the Government borrow to finance nationally significant infrastructure supporting productivity or Singapore's sustainability.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The purpose of the Act is to enable the Government to borrow and to finance nationally significant infrastructure to support or improve national productivity or Singapore's economic, environmental or social sustainability.

sections.label: Health spending and fiscal sustainability
sections.summary: Rising health expenditure with an ageing population makes tax revenue capacity important; fiscal sustainability requires primary surpluses covering public debt.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: With health expenditure rising as a share of gross domestic product (GDP) in tandem with an ageing population, having the capacity to raise tax revenue to fund such spending will become important.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Government Budget at any point in time is fiscally sustainable if the expected present value of primary surpluses, which do not include interest payments, is at least as large as the size of the public debt.

sections.label: GST rate increase plan
sections.summary: The Government announced in Budget 2021 that it plans to raise GST from 7% to 9% any time from 2020 to 2025.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Government has announced in Budget 2021 that it plans to raise the GST rate from 7% to 9% any time from 2020 to 2025.

sections.label: Safe interest rate and fiscal sustainability
sections.summary: Unexpected rises in the safe interest rate can affect fiscal sustainability, requiring tax increases or spending cuts to re-establish it.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: While the safe interest rate is currently low and expected to be low for some time, unexpected events that raise the safe interest rate can affect fiscal sustainability.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Data showed that in the early 1980s – the first half of the decade of the 1980s – the safe interest rate experienced a sharp spike that caused a fiscal crisis in many emerging economies and posed budgetary challenges for some advanced economies as well since the cost of servicing public debt sharply increased.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In order to re-establish fiscal sustainability in the event that the safe interest rate rises, it is necessary to either raise taxes or to cut spending.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: We must maintain the reputation that we have built up over the years for good financial management of our fiscal affairs.

sections.label: Singapore borrowing and AAA rating
sections.summary: Singapore's AAA rating allows borrowing at favourable interest rates, and investing these funds in infrastructure will stimulate future growth to service loans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: In other countries, in addition to borrowing money, some governments had resorted to printing money, commercialising public services and levying taxes in order to afford development works.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: We are fortunate that Singapore's AAA rating enables us to borrow at favourable interest rates, particularly in the current economic environment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I am confident that using these funds to invest in our infrastructure development will stimulate future economic growth, which will enable us to service and return the borrowed money.

sections.label: Servicing loans through project revenue
sections.summary: Loans can be partly serviced through revenue from infrastructure services like tolls and fees, with more revenue from foreign parties reducing future generations' burden.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: How can we levy taxes for infrastructure projects when we are already trying so hard to minimise taxes?

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: It is possible to partly service the loans through revenue collected from services provided by the infrastructure such as via tolls and fees.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: A portion of the repayment will come from users of the projects who can be both local and foreign.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: It would be less of a burden on our future generations if more of the revenue could be generated from foreign or external parties while ensuring that the services provided fulfil all demands without conflict or competition.

sections.label: Reserves and Net Investment Income
sections.summary: Singapore's financial assets reached $1.35 trillion by March 2020, with about $40 billion yearly Net Investment Income funding infrastructure and social spending.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Today, the total financial assets owned by our country has reached $1.35 trillion by end of March 2020.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Even without touching the principal of the reserves, the Net Investment Income of about $40 billion a year from the reserves is enough to fund the infrastructural projects and social spending increases, especially those in the healthcare area, into the foreseeable future.

sections.label: GIC/MAS returns and SINGA loans
sections.summary: The speaker expects GIC/MAS to earn at least 2% above SINGA borrowing costs and wants SINGA loans in Singapore dollars.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: For better financial efficiency, I would expect GIC/MAS to generate a higher return of at least 2% more than the borrowing cost of the SINGA loans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The SINGA loans should also be issued as Singapore dollar-denominated securities to reduce foreign exchange exposure and to broaden and deepen our bond markets.

sections.label: SINGA loans, accountability, PSP fiscal plan
sections.summary: The S$700 billion is reinvested abroad, SINGA loans are real debts, and PSP seeks more funds for middle-class Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: But strictly speaking, these are not debts because this S$700 billion is reinvested in the financial assets of foreign countries through the GIC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: It is only the SINGA loans that will be our real debts because these loans will be used for significant infrastructure projects.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: I therefore hope that the Government will increase the accountability for SINGA loans and report to Parliament regularly on the progress of these projects.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, with no real lack of fiscal resources and SINGA as an additional funding source, the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) calls on the Government to review our long-term fiscal plan and allocate more funds to alleviate the financial pressures of our middle class Singaporeans and help them improve their quality of life.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: This is necessary because the future of our country depends on a resilient Singaporean Core of skilled workers and motivated entrepreneurs.

sections.label: $90 billion limit versus past Acts
sections.summary: The $90 billion limit is about 20% of GDP, lower than the past six Development Loan Acts at near 40%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: One, the $90 billion limit is about 20% of current Gross Domestic Product (GDP) which is lower than the past six Development Loan Acts, which was near 40% of GDP.

sections.label: Questions on project criteria and bonds
sections.summary: The speaker asks how the $4 billion minimum project sum was set, for the risk matrix, and whether bond duration matches project payback.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Two, how did the setting of a minimum project qualification sum at $4 billion come about and what would be the considerations in the future for adjustments of this minimum sum qualification criterion?

sentences.speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Three, could the risk and benefit assessment matrix that the Government intends to use for deciding on projects be shared with Parliament, please?

sentences.speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Four, will the duration of the issued bonds dovetail with the payback period of the project to prevent a scenario where a bond needs to be extended with higher interest rates and, thereby, adding more expenditure to recurrent Government Budgets?

sections.label: 50-year infrastructure safeguard
sections.summary: One safeguard requires infrastructure developments to last at least 50 years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: One safeguard is that the infrastructure developments must last for at least 50 years.

sections.label: SINGA Bill borrowing safeguards
sections.summary: The passage states the SINGA Bill format suits intergenerational distributive justice and notes a $90 billion gross borrowing limit and $5 billion yearly interest threshold.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: But when it comes to infrastructure developments which lasts for generations, to achieve – in the words of Prof Hoon Hian Teck – intergenerational distributive justice, then it makes sense to consider the format that we have in the SINGA Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: There are two other safeguards which I thought was laudatory: the gross borrowing limit of $90 billion, which is about 20% of our Singapore's GDP, as well as the interest threshold of $5 billion per year and this limits the Government's ability to borrow if interest rates go up.

sections.label: Constitution Article 144 approval
sections.summary: The passage states Article 144 of the Constitution is engaged and the President gave in-principle approval, agreeing to a $90 billion borrowing limit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: As mentioned by the hon Deputy Prime Minister, Article 144 of the Constitution is engaged, and he highlighted that the in-principle approval of the President has been obtained for the passing of this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: And it was specifically mentioned that Her Excellency agreed to a borrowing limit of $90 billion.

sections.label: Green bonds on public projects
sections.summary: The passage states the Deputy Prime Minister said in February 2021 that Singapore will issue green bonds on select public infrastructure projects, with up to $19 billion identified.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The hon Deputy Prime Minister Heng mentioned in February 2021 that Singapore will issue green bonds on select public infrastructure projects, with up to $19 billion of public sector green projects already identified.

sections.label: Development expenditure and depreciation
sections.summary: The passage gives a $1 billion, 50-year project example with $20 million annual depreciation and lists development expenditure figures for FY2018 to 2021.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: As an example, a $1 billion project today with a useful life of 50 years is charged to the financial statements at 2% annually, which represents a $20 million annual depreciation charge.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In FY2018 and FY2019, actual total development expenditure was $20.3 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, while the revised development expenditure in 2020 was $16.4 billion and the estimated expenditure in 2021 will be $19.9 billion.

sections.label: MRT and sewage projects
sections.summary: The passage states that new MRT lines, line extensions and the Deep Tunnel Sewage System would fall under the scope of SINGA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The new MRT lines, such as the next phases of the Thomson-East Coast Line, the Jurong Regional Line and Cross Island Line, as well as the extension of current lines, such as the North-East Line, Downtown Line and projects, such as the Deep Tunnel Sewage System as mentioned by Deputy Prime Minister Heng, are projects that would fall under the scope of SINGA.

sections.label: Fifty-year useful life requirement
sections.summary: The passage states that these projects need to have a useful life of at least 50 years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Third, I note that these projects need to have a useful life of at least 50 years.

sections.label: Green infrastructure share of SINGA
sections.summary: The Member asks the Deputy Prime Minister how much of the $90 billion set aside for SINGA would go to green infrastructure.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In trying to keep in line with these aims, I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister, out of the $90 billion set aside for SINGA, how much of this would be set aside for green infrastructure?

sections.label: $90 billion loan limit
sections.summary: The first question concerns the $90 billion loan limit that has been put in place.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The first question is on the $90 billion loan limit which has been put in place.

sections.label: Interest and yield on loan limit
sections.summary: Total effective interest of $5 billion implies a total yield to maturity of 5.6% on the $90 billion loan limit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: On the total effective interest paid or payable of $5 billion, that would imply a total yield to maturity of 5.6% on the loan limit of $90 billion.

sections.label: Projects below qualifying amount
sections.summary: The projects, despite their size and value, hardly come close to the qualifying amount of $4 billion or more.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Despite the size and value that these projects bring, they hardly come close to the qualifying amount of $4 billion or more.

sections.label: Past borrowing and seniors' retirement funds
sections.summary: Since the 1990s the Government has not borrowed for other infrastructure besides Changi Terminals 1 and 2 and the first MRT project, and more than half of seniors appear to lack sufficient retirement funds.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Besides Changi Airport Terminals 1 and 2 and the first MRT project, the Government has not borrowed to fund other infrastructure projects since the 1990s.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In essence, the generation that came before us has borne a significant cost of infrastructure development upfront for our benefit without having the cost spread equitably across generations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Despite a lifetime of hard work and contributions to our nation, sadly more than half of our seniors do not appear to have sufficient funds to retire comfortably.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Needless to say, we should never contemplate taking any future decision that could potentially add to their tax burden.

sections.label: Hard versus soft infrastructure investment
sections.summary: The Member argues that favourable interest rates are offered for hard infrastructure but not soft infrastructure, though returns on soft infrastructure dominate those of hard.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: The context is that the interest rates are currently low.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: So, when we say that we want to invest in infrastructure, hard infrastructure, but not soft infrastructure, it seems like we are only willing to offer the terms of favourable interest rates for physical capital and not human capital.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: For me, that is like saying that we think it is equally important to educate both our son and our daughter, but sure, we will finance Ah Boy's schooling but Ah Girl, you go work so that you can pay for your school fees.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: And the other point which is worth pointing out is something that other Members, including Prof Hoon, mentioned, which is that we always need to think about the returns when we invest in a project.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: I agree with this and this is why in my speech, I demonstrated that returns on soft infrastructure actually dominate those of hard, which is yet another reason why we want to invest in soft infrastructure in this Bill.

sections.label: Government long-term infrastructure plans
sections.summary: The Government has bold long-term plans for Changi Airport Terminal 5, a third runway, a Tuas mega seaport and MRT expansion to anchor Singapore's development into SG100.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: So, my first observation is about this Government's long-term plan for our national infrastructure.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: There are very bold, ambitious plans, for Changi Airport Terminal 5 and a third runway, for a mega seaport in Tuas, for a massive expansion in our MRT rail network, and much more, all in turn to anchor Singapore's next phase of development, well into SG100.

sections.label: World Bank loan for container terminal
sections.summary: The Government borrowed $45 million from the World Bank and the container terminal was completed in 1972.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: The Government then had to borrow $45 million from the World Bank, a very handsome sum back then, and the container terminal was completed in 1972.

sections.label: Budget growth from 2003
sections.summary: The Budget grew from $6.5 billion in 2003 to $12 billion and $13 billion in recent years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: From $6.5 billion in the 2003 Budget, to $12 billion, $13 billion in recent years.

sections.label: Figures from 2003 to 2019
sections.summary: The figures rose from $2 billion in 2003 to $6 billion in 2013 and $12 billion in 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: From $2 billion in 2003, to $6 billion in 2013, to $12 billion in 2019.

sections.label: Lower cap on total borrowings
sections.summary: The speaker's first suggestion is to lower the cap on total borrowings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: My first suggestion is to lower the cap on total borrowings.

sections.label: Lowering borrowing cap to $50 billion
sections.summary: To maintain public confidence, the speaker suggests lowering the initial cap to $50 billion, roughly 10% of GDP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: Ninety billion dollars is not quite enough to run the country to the ground, but certainly enough to cause a rather bad bout of indigestion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: And so, to maintain public confidence, I suggest that the initial cap be lowered to $50 billion, which would represent roughly 10% of GDP.

sections.label: Initial cap of $2.5 billion
sections.summary: The speaker suggests limiting the initial cap to $2.5 billion, about 10% of recent annual development outlays, to signal prudence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: To signal prudence, I suggest that the initial cap be limited to $2.5 billion, or roughly 10% of recent annual development outlays.

sections.label: Lowering qualifying project limit
sections.summary: The speaker suggests lowering the qualifying limit for projects so qualifying projects of national significance can be more inclusive and flexible, given safeguards on total borrowing and interests.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: Since we have the safeguards on total borrowing and total interests, I suggest we lower the qualifying limit for projects so that the scope of qualifying projects of national significance can be made more inclusive and more flexible.

sections.label: Bill safeguards and borrowing limits
sections.summary: The Bill sets a $90 billion gross borrowing limit, a $5 billion annual interest rate threshold, and requires legislative amendments to raise more loans under SINGA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: The Bill has also importantly spelt out crystal-clear clauses for safeguards.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: There will be a gross borrowing limit of $90 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: The Government cannot raise more than this amount in loans under SINGA without legislative amendments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: There is also an annual interest rate threshold of $5 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: These measures will ensure the future generations will not end up with burdensome financing costs.

sections.label: Germany green bonds and borrowing rate
sections.summary: Germany's green bonds were priced at a premium and had lower yields and volatility; the speaker asks for project size and timing, noting a 5.5% borrowing rate at maximum borrowing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Recently, Germany issued green bond counterparts to its 10-year and five-year conventional bonds.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: In both cases, the green bonds were priced at a premium when issued.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: They seem to have consistently maintained lower yields as well as exhibiting lower volatility than their conventional versions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Can the Deputy Prime Minister also share more information about the project size, timing and so on, if possible?

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: If they are related, assuming that we reach the maximum borrowing of $90 billion based on the $5 billion annual interest payment, the borrowing rate is 5.5% per annum.

sections.label: Minimum project cost of $4 billion
sections.summary: The speaker questions why the minimum project cost is $4 billion, noting the Sports Hub incurred only $1.3 billion in construction costs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Another question is why is the minimum project cost set at $4 billion?

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: To put this figure in context, a massive project like the iconic Sports Hub incurred only $1.3 billion in construction costs.

sections.label: Green share of SINGA bonds
sections.summary: The passage asks how much of the SINGA bonds will be green.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: How much of the SINGA bonds will be green?

sections.label: Borrowing limit and interest threshold
sections.summary: Safeguards cap gross borrowing at $90 billion and annual interest at $5 billion, changeable only by a new Bill in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Key safeguards include the $90 billion gross limit on borrowing and an annual interest threshold of $5 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Future changes to the gross borrowing limit and annual interest threshold can only be made by introducing a new Bill in Parliament.

sections.label: Green bonds and climate adaptation
sections.summary: Green bonds could fund $19 billion of public sector green projects and climate adaptation structures such as sea walls and dykes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: For example, these green bonds could be used to fund some of the $19 billion of public sector green projects identified in the Singapore Green Plan 2030.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Thirdly, I understand that there are plans for SINGA to finance the building of climate adaptation structures, such as sea walls, dykes, floodgates, barrages and coastal pumping stations to mitigate the risks of rising sea levels.

sections.label: Borrowing to spread infrastructure costs
sections.summary: The Government can finance MRT lines, climate adaptation infrastructure and sewerage systems through borrowings to spread lumpy costs over time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Given the need to continue to develop our MRT lines, infrastructure to adapt to climate change as well as sewerage systems, it is logical and a sensible thing for our Government to finance these projects through borrowings to spread the lumpiness of the cost to match the benefits that will accrue over time.

sections.label: Interest cap on SINGA bonds
sections.summary: Clause 5(1)(b) limits total effective interest paid to no more than S$5 billion, an implied cap of around 5.5%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Clause 5 (1)(b) limits the total effective interest rate paid on the securities issued under this legislation to be no more than S$5 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Effectively, the Bill provides an implied interest cap of around 5.5% against the total SINGA bonds of S$90 billion.

sections.label: Longer tenor risk-free curve
sections.summary: Longer tenor SINGA bonds can help build a longer term risk-free curve for pricing long-dated projects such as project finance loans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: With SINGA bonds issued with longer tenors, this can help build out a longer term risk-free curve which financial institutions need for referencing the pricing of long-dated projects, such as project finance loans as an example.

sections.label: Debt dynamics and borrowing costs
sections.summary: Borrowing for infrastructure can lower debt-to-GDP if GDP grows faster, but marginal borrowing costs can rise abruptly when refinancing.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: The infrastructure projects that the SINGA bonds are expected to fund, whether for new rail lines or climate adaptation, will surely boost productivity, growth and the sustainability of our economy over the long term.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: If we can grow GDP faster, taking on debt to fund public investment in nationally significant infrastructure, under the current low interest rate environment, can in fact lead to lower debt-to-GDP in the long term.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: The bigger the interest rates-growth differential, the more favourable the debt dynamics.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: However, IMF studies have shown that marginal borrowing costs often rise abruptly and sharply after long periods of low differentials, and it is marginal borrowing costs which really matters when it comes to refinancing.

sections.label: SINGA borrowing capitalisation change
sections.summary: The passage notes a change to capitalisation of expenditures financed through borrowings under SINGA.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Perhaps, the most noteworthy thing here is really the change to capitalisation of expenditures financed through borrowings under SINGA.

sections.label: Borrowing purposes and SSGS
sections.summary: Borrowings under LTBA and GSA are for specific policy purposes, with 71% being SSGS supporting Singaporeans' retirement needs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Today, we borrow under the Local Treasury Bills Act or LTBA and the Government Securities Act or GSA only for specific policy purposes such as for market development, meeting the investment needs of CPF, and liquidity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: In fact, the majority of our borrowings, about 71%, is made up of the Special Singapore Government Securities (SSGS), which are issued primarily to support the retirement needs of Singaporeans.

sections.label: OECD net government debt rise
sections.summary: Average net government debt among OECD countries rose from 65% of GDP in 2019 to 80% in 2020.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: For instance, the average net government debt amongst OECD countries rose from 65% of GDP in 2019 to 80% in 2020.

sections.label: Credit rating agencies on Singapore
sections.summary: Credit rating agencies acknowledged Singapore's fiscal position and credit rating remain strong despite planned new borrowings for long-term infrastructure.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Even with the planned introduction of new borrowings to finance long-term major infrastructure, the credit rating agencies acknowledged that Singapore’s fiscal position and credit rating remain strong.

sections.label: Borrowing limited to large infrastructure
sections.summary: Prudence is exercised by limiting borrowing to infrastructure projects with a total qualifying cost of at least $4 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: One way we are exercising prudence is by limiting borrowing to infrastructure projects that have a total qualifying cost of at least $4 billion.

sections.label: Reviewing $4 billion threshold
sections.summary: The $4 billion threshold captures major development needs, and the government is open to reviewing it in future if necessary.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: The $4 billion threshold captures major, lumpy development needs that form the upcoming "hump" above our baseline development expenditure, and are important to our national interests, as I have explained earlier on.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: We are mindful that our infrastructure needs will evolve as our economy grows.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Hence, we are open to reviewing the $4 billion threshold in the future if necessary.

sections.label: Who pays for borrowing
sections.summary: Neither Jamus Lim nor Louis Chua addressed who will pay for the borrowing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: In talking about all the spending, neither Assoc Prof Jamus Lim nor Mr Louis Chua addressed the question of who is going to pay for this borrowing.

sections.label: Debt financing and expenditure
sections.summary: Most developed countries debt financing end with more debt, and over 30% of expenditure goes to MOE and MOH.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Most developed countries that go into debt financing just end up with more debt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: I want to remind Members that we spend more than 30% of our expenditure each year on MOE and MOH, and that share is expected to rise.

sections.label: Government share of healthcare spending
sections.summary: Government financing for national healthcare expenditure rose from 35% in 2011 to 46% in 2018.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: I mentioned that I would speak about the share of Government financing for just national healthcare expenditure alone.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: It was 35% in 2011 and 46% in 2018; and likely to rise further – so, an 11-percentage point increase in just seven years.

sections.label: Drawing past reserves for COVID-19
sections.summary: Up to $53.7 billion is expected to be drawn from past reserves over FY2020 and FY2021 for COVID-19.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Indeed, with the President's concurrence, up to $53.7 billion is expected to be drawn from our past reserves over FY2020 and FY2021 to respond to the COVID-19 crisis.

sections.label: Tabling Bill to consider borrowing
sections.summary: The Bill is tabled to consider borrowing if necessary to emerge stronger from the crisis.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: We will continue to monitor the economic and public health outlook closely and study this option carefully.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: It is in this context that I am tabling this Bill and to consider borrowing, if necessary, to emerge stronger from this generational crisis.

sections.label: Ninety billion dollar limit
sections.summary: Ninety billion dollars is a sizeable limit, as Mr Xie Yao Quan pointed out.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Ninety billion dollars is a sizeable limit, as Mr Xie Yao Quan pointed out.

sections.label: Canada debt ceiling comparison
sections.summary: Canada's recurrent debt ceiling is about 51% of its GDP, and a $90 billion gross borrowing limit is prudent and sustainable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: For example, Canada, which also has good credit rating, has a recurrent debt ceiling of 1.17 trillion Canadian dollars, which is about 51% of their GDP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: So, when we compare with our own past experiences and those of other countries, a gross borrowing limit of $90 billion is prudent and sustainable and can meet our needs.

sections.label: $5 billion interest cost cap
sections.summary: A $5 billion cap limits interest cost to around 1% of GDP in 2020 at current market prices.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: As I have mentioned in my speech earlier, $5 billion caps our interest cost at around 1% of our GDP in 2020 at current market prices.

sections.label: 1998 SGS interest rates
sections.summary: Interest rates for 10-year Singapore Government Securities reached 5.87% in 1998.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: For example, interest rates for 10-year Singapore Government Securities (SGS) reached 5.87% in 1998.

sections.label: $90 billion borrowing cap timing
sections.summary: The cap will not bind initially as spending is limited, but may bind closer to the $90 billion limit in a high interest rate environment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: As we are ramping up infrastructure quite evenly over the next 10 to 15 years, the cap will not be binding as our initial spend is more limited.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: The next five years we are likely to utilise less than $30 billion but it is prudent that we size this cap early.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: If we issue bonds in the next few years, when rates are expected to be low, this will help reduce the overall effective interest cost even if rates go up in the future.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Hence, the cap will likely be more binding when we are closer to the $90 billion gross borrowing limit and if we are in a particularly high interest rate environment in the future.

sections.label: Asset depreciation period cap
sections.summary: As a safeguard, the depreciation period for assets will be capped at either 50 or 70 years, rounded down from useful life.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: As an additional safeguard for prudence, we intend to cap the depreciation period for the assets at either 50 or 70 years, rounded down from its useful life.

sections.label: Green bond issuance plans
sections.summary: Up to $19 billion of green bonds will be issued over five years, with first Green SGS (Infrastructure) issuances expected from FY2022.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: They will serve as a reference for the domestic green bond market, deepen the market liquidity for green bonds, attract green investors and anchor Singapore as the green finance hub.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: We will issue up to $19 billion of green bonds over the next five years for a start.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: For Green SGS (Infrastructure) issued under the SINGA, we expect the first issuances from FY2022 onwards.

sections.label: Tuas Nexus climate change project
sections.summary: Tuas Nexus maximises energy and resource recovery in waste and used water treatment, saving over 200,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide annually, equal to taking 42,500 cars off the road.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Mr Louis Ng will be happy to know that the Tuas Nexus is one of the projects to help mitigate climate change.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: It maximises energy and resource recovery in the solid waste and used water treatment processes, leading to carbon savings of more than 200,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide annually.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: So, this is equivalent to taking 42,500 cars off the road.

sections.label: Borrowing and GST rate increase
sections.summary: Borrowing for recurrent spending would raise debt levels, so the GST rate still needs to be raised for structural increases in healthcare and social spending as the population ages.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Borrowing for recurrent spending will only mean that we will end up with higher and higher debt levels.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: So, therefore, there will still be a need to raise the GST rate, to raise recurrent revenues for structural increases in healthcare and social spending as our population ages.

sections.label: SINGA borrowing and fiscal space
sections.summary: Borrowing for nationally significant infrastructure is excluded from the $90 billion borrowing limits, and SINGA creates fiscal space of 0.8% of GDP annually, around $4 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Well, we will not be borrowing for recurrent expenditure related to nationally significant infrastructure, such as cost of repair and maintenance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: So, this cost will be excluded from counting towards the $90 billion borrowing limits.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Third, Ms Foo asked, to quantify the fiscal space created from this accounting treatment, what is estimated to be the amount of taxes that would have had to be raised to fund such long-term expenditure if this was made under the current annual expense approach and does that mean that we will have more fiscal room?

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: I have said in my main speech earlier on that borrowing under SINGA will, I quote, "lower our annual average development expenditure over the next decade from around 5% of our GDP to 4.2% of our GDP after taking account depreciation and borrowing costs." So, in other words, on average, SINGA will create fiscal space of 0.8% of our GDP annually, in the next decade after taking into account the depreciation and borrowing costs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: And this is around $4 billion in current dollars.

sections.label: Questions on fiscal resources and reserves
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Deputy Prime Minister about $128 billion in fiscal resources, $1.35 trillion in financial assets, indirect taxes, and a 20-year expenditure forecast.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: One, I will ask the Deputy Prime Minister: do you agree that this year, fiscal resources amount to $128 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: We do not care how you classify that resources into revenue, but you have $128 billion; $39 billion of NIRC; $12 billion of land sales and $77 billion of taxes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Two, while you refused to announce the accurate figure for the reserves, the Government publishes Government financial statements every year; and as of March 2020, the total financial assets reported on the financial statement was $1.35 trillion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: One question I want to ask you is: why do you not go to our constituency and tell the constituents, "Please pay more taxes; you will get more from the Government." Have you taken into consideration all the indirect taxes when you presented your conclusion?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: And fourth, for the expenditures that the Government is trying to incur, are you prepared to give a 20-year forecast of all the expenditures that are going to come?

sections.label: Land sales and NIRC rules
sections.summary: Land sale proceeds are not used for recurrent spending and go into past reserves, while only up to 50% of NIRC is taken.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: First, you quoted the figure of $128 billion and quoted $38 billion of NIRC and $12 billion of land sales.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Again, I said in this Parliament, over and over again, please, read the Hansard, that land sale proceeds are not be used for recurrent spending.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: We have a Reserve Protection Framework, where land sales go into past reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Past reserves are then invested, and we have the elected Presidency to ensure that the Reserve Protection Framework is working as it should, working properly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: And as for NIRC, again, and I have said it before, that we only take up to 50% of the NIRC and we are already doing that.

sections.label: Raising GST to 9%
sections.summary: The speaker argues that GST needs to be raised from 7% to 9%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Which is why I have argued that we need to raise GST from 7% to 9%.

sections.label: Long-term projection limits
sections.summary: The speaker warned that 20-year projections are not possible because contingent events like COVID-19 always occur.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: When you asked whether I could provide projections for the next 20 years, I warned that it is not possible to project over such a long term because there will always be contingent events like COVID-19.

sections.label: Structural drivers of expenditure
sections.summary: The speaker says the best approach is to examine structural drivers of expenditures such as healthcare.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: What we can do, to the best of our ability, is to look at structural drivers that will drive certain expenditures, such as healthcare.

sections.label: IMF revenue classification standard
sections.summary: The classification of what constitutes revenue available for spending follows the International Monetary Fund's international standard.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: It is not my classification or MOF's classification that this constitutes revenue available for spending, and this does not.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: It follows the international standard set out by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

sections.label: Net asset position and reserves
sections.summary: The speaker says clear principles define countable spending, and Singapore's net asset position means reserves inherited from forefathers pay debt servicing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: It has a set of clear principles as to what will constitute proper spending and what can be counted and what cannot be counted and so on.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: And because we are in a net asset position – we are not in a net debt position, debt servicing costs and so on – as I said in my speech, instead of us using current revenue to pay for debt servicing incurred by earlier generations, we have been in an extremely fortunate situation that we inherited that legacy, those reserves, from our forefathers.

sections.label: Higher cohort participation rate
sections.summary: The Government raised the funded cohort participation rate to 40%, set up two new universities and invests in adult education.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Just one data point, a simple data point: we increased the cohort participation rate that is funded by the Government to 40%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: We set up two new Universities and, right now, we are also investing more in adult education, in SkillsFuture and so on.

sections.label: Limits of spending money
sections.summary: The speaker says consistent investment by parents and students is needed, so spending more money alone cannot achieve great outcomes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: It takes consistent investment of time, effort and energy by parents and by students.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: So, to just simply think that we can achieve great outcomes by spending more money is just wrong.

sections.label: Education spending and results
sections.summary: An education minister warned against assuming that spending more money will produce better results.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
sentences.text: Again, one education minister told me, "Please do not make the mistake that we have made, which is to assume that when we spend more, we will get better results.
